metadata.domain: University study planning and programming coursework support
metadata.description: Regex-driven intents and response templates for the CM2015 Programming with Data midterm chatbot.

responses: Nice to meet you, {name}. I will remember your name while this chat is running.
Thanks, {name}. I can now personalise study and project-planning responses for you.

intents.description: Store the course or module the user is studying.
responses: Got it{name_phrase}: I will treat {course} as your current course context.
Course memory updated to {course}. Ask me for a project plan, revision strategy, or test-case ideas.

intents.description: Store a simple preference to demonstrate dynamic memory substitution.
responses: I have stored {color} as your favourite colour. I can reuse it in later responses as a memory example.
Memory updated: favourite colour = {color}.
Hello{name_phrase}. I am StudyBuddy. I can help with planning, revision, Python concepts, deadlines, and test cases.
Hi{name_phrase}. Tell me what you are working on, or ask for help with regex, JSON, testing, or study planning.
Goodbye{name_phrase}. Good luck with {course}.
See you later{name_phrase}. Keep your next study task small and specific.
You are welcome{name_phrase}.
Glad it helped{name_phrase}. Ask for another plan, explanation, or test case whenever you need one.
I am StudyBuddy, a rule-based university study assistant. I use regex patterns, JSON intents, preprocessing, sentiment scoring, and short-term memory.
I can help plan coursework, explain programming concepts, suggest revision routines, generate test-case ideas, and reflect back stored memory.

intents.description: Advice on submissions, deadlines, and urgent planning.
responses: For a deadline{deadline_phrase}, use a three-pass plan: make the minimum working version, test it, then improve the report and comments.
Prioritise runnable code first, then test cases, then polish. Keep every required file in the same folder so relative paths work.
Build a checklist: notebook runs top-to-bottom, JSON loads correctly, main loop exits on 'exit' or 'quit', tests pass, and the report matches the implementation.

intents.description: Break coursework into stages and milestones.
responses: Suggested roadmap{name_phrase}: 1) define intents, 2) store patterns/responses in JSON, 3) add regex matching, 4) add preprocessing, 5) add memory and dynamic responses, 6) test and report.
Make the next milestone concrete: one JSON intent, one matching function, one response-generation function, and one test that proves it works.
For {course}, separate implementation evidence from explanation evidence: code cells show behaviour; the report explains design choices and reflection.

intents.description: Extract useful keywords from a user sentence.
responses: The strongest keywords I found are: {keywords}.
Keyword summary: {keywords}. These are based on tokenisation, stop-word removal, and stemming.

intents.description: Explain Python concepts relevant to the chatbot.
responses: For {topic}, keep the code modular: one function should do one job, take clear inputs, and return a clear result.
In this chatbot, {topic} supports maintainability: JSON stores data, regex detects intent, and functions keep the main loop readable.
A useful pattern is: load data -> preprocess input -> find intent -> update memory -> choose and format a response.
Use tests that check intent tags, memory updates, and absence of raw placeholders such as {name} in final responses.
Good test cases include a normal input, a varied spelling or punctuation input, and an unknown input that should trigger fallback safely.
Test behaviour, not random wording. Because responses are random, assert the detected intent and key facts rather than one exact sentence.

intents.description: Respond to stress, overwhelm, and low motivation.
responses: I am detecting a {sentiment_label} tone. Shrink the task: choose the next 10-minute action, such as fixing one regex or writing one test.
Start with the smallest visible win{name_phrase}: open the notebook, run all cells, and note the first error or missing feature.
When the work feels too large, split it into code, data, tests, and report. Finish one small item before switching.
Use active recall: close your notes, write what you remember, then check the gaps. Repeat the weakest topic first.
Try a 25-minute focus block: one small goal, no switching tasks, then a 5-minute break and a one-line summary.
For programming revision, read code, predict the output, run it, and then change one part to test your understanding.

intents.description: Summarise short-term memory stored during the session.
responses: Current memory: name={name}, course={course}, favourite colour={color}, last deadline={deadline}.
I currently know: name={name}; course={course}; favourite colour={color}; deadline context={deadline}.

intents.description: Default response when no intent matches.
responses: I am not sure I matched that. Try asking about planning, deadlines, regex, JSON, tests, revision, or memory.
I did not find a confident intent. Rephrase with a keyword such as 'deadline', 'project plan', 'regex', 'test case', or 'revision'.
